title: Hyponatremia: working it up and correcting it safely

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on the European and US expert panel hyponatremia guidelines. Not tied to an article; review before trusting.

questions.q: What is the first test that sorts out a low sodium?
questions.why: A low osmolality confirms true hypotonic hyponatremia. A normal or high osmolality points to pseudohyponatremia from lipids or protein, or to hyperglycaemia.

questions.q: By how much is the measured sodium corrected upward for each 100 mg/dL of glucose above normal?
questions.why: Glucose pulls water into the blood and dilutes the sodium. Once the glucose is treated the sodium rises on its own, which matters when judging the rate of correction.

questions.q: Which findings support SIADH in a euvolemic patient with hypotonic hyponatremia?
questions.why: The diagnosis is one of exclusion; low uric acid supports it. Common causes are lung and brain disease, pain, nausea, SSRIs, carbamazepine and small cell cancer.

questions.q: What is the maximum safe rise in sodium over 24 hours in chronic hyponatremia?
questions.why: Faster correction risks osmotic demyelination, which appears days later and is largely irreversible. Some guidance allows up to 10 in low-risk patients; 8 is the safe number to remember.

questions.q: Which factors raise the risk of osmotic demyelination during correction?
questions.why: Liver disease is the other classic one. In these patients the 24-hour limit is dropped to 4 to 6 mEq/L and the sodium is checked every 4 hours.

questions.q: A patient with a sodium of 116 is having a seizure. What is the treatment?
questions.a: A 100 to 150 mL bolus of 3% saline over 10 to 20 minutes, repeated up to three times
d: Normal saline at 250 mL per hour
questions.why: The aim is a rise of 4 to 6 mEq/L in the first hours, which stops the seizures. The 24-hour limit still applies to the total.

questions.q: Hypovolemic hyponatremia from vomiting and diarrhoea. What is the treatment?
questions.why: Once volume is restored the ADH stimulus switches off and the kidneys excrete free water, so the sodium can rise faster than expected; it is monitored closely.

questions.q: Which is the first-line treatment for hyponatremia caused by SIADH?
questions.why: Isotonic saline can worsen SIADH because the kidney keeps the water and excretes the salt. Salt tablets with a loop diuretic, urea, or tolvaptan are the next steps.

questions.q: Sodium has risen 10 mEq/L in 12 hours after treatment. What is done?
questions.a: Give desmopressin and free water to bring the sodium back down
questions.why: Deliberate relowering within the first day reduces the risk of demyelination. Some units give desmopressin from the start alongside hypertonic saline to make the correction predictable.

questions.q: Which class of diuretic most often causes hyponatremia?
questions.why: Thiazides impair urinary dilution while loop diuretics do not, which is why furosemide is used, not hydrochlorothiazide, when a hyponatraemic patient needs diuresis.

questions.q: Which endocrine conditions must be excluded before diagnosing SIADH?
questions.why: Both cause a euvolemic hyponatremia that looks identical on urine tests. A morning cortisol and a TSH are part of every work-up.

questions.q: A heavy beer drinker who eats little has a sodium of 118 with a urine osmolality of 60 mOsm/kg. What is the mechanism?
questions.a: Too little solute intake to excrete the water load
questions.why: Beer potomania and the tea-and-toast diet correct quickly once solute is given, so the risk is over-correction rather than under-treatment.
